name: Back shaver

lead: A back shaver gives a smooth, clean back and shoulders without needing someone else to do it. The result is visible immediately.

It is a razor or trimmer on an extended handle; the long handle extends reach while the head works like an ordinary razor or trimmer, cutting hair at or near the skin. It is a niche grooming tool with no dedicated studies.

paras: Users shave or trim their own back and shoulders at home, repeating as hair returns. Because the area is hard to see, people often use a mirror or take extra care with passes.
General clinical sources describe razor-related ingrown hairs and irritation, particularly with curly hair. No data specific to back shavers exist.

angle.text: An extended-handle razor or trimmer lets you remove or shorten hair on your own back and shoulders for a clean look without help. The result is immediate.

lead: A back shaver is a razor or trimmer attached to an extended handle so that a person can remove or shorten hair on their own back and shoulders without help. It is a grooming tool within the broader category of body hair removal.

No studies or encyclopedic articles specifically about back shavers were found. Background on body hair removal comes from general sources describing why some men shave, and from clinical sources on razor-related skin problems.
infobox: Razor or trimmer on extended handle
Removing hair from the back and shoulders

paras: The defining feature is a long handle, which lets the user reach areas that are hard to see or access. Designs include manual razor-head models and electric trimmer-head models; specifics vary by brand and are not documented in the sources consulted.
Wikipedia records that some bodybuilders and athletes remove body hair to show muscle definition or reduce friction.[1] Back hair is one of the areas people mention when discussing body grooming.

Razor shaving can cause ingrown hairs and inflammation (pseudofolliculitis), especially in people with curly or coarse hair; clinical sources list sharp single-blade razors, shaving in the direction of growth and avoiding very close shaves among common recommendations.[2] The back is hard to inspect, and no studies of this tool's injury rate were found.
